claim: The mouse has been recognized as a valuable and economic model animal for biomedical research in social behaviors.
source: The mouse has been recognized as a valuable and economic model animal for biomedical research in social behaviors
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific citation, representing accepted scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Currently available food competition paradigms for mice remain limited.
source: however, currently available food competition paradigms for mice remain limited.
evidence: This is an assertion made by the authors based on their review of existing literature and methods.

claim: The FPCT was designed to provide researchers with a choice of new food competition paradigm.
source: This food pellet competition test (FPCT) was designed to (1) provide researchers with a choice of new food competition paradigm
evidence: This is a stated purpose of the study design.

claim: The FPCT was designed to expose psychological factors influencing the establishment and/or expression of social status in mice by avoiding direct physical competition between contenders.
source: This food pellet competition test (FPCT) was designed to (1) provide researchers with a choice of new food competition paradigm and (2) expose psychological factors influencing the establishment and/or expression of social status in mice by avoiding direct physical competition between contenders.
evidence: This is a stated design goal of the FPCT paradigm.

claim: The authors hypothesized inconsistency of rankings of mice tested by FPCT, tube test, and WST as they possess different targets for mice to compete and different factors determining competitiveness.
source: We hypothesized inconsistency of rankings of mice tested by FPCT, tube test, and WST as they possess different targets for mice to compete and different factors determining competitiveness.
evidence: This is the explicitly stated hypothesis of the study.

claim: Application of FPCT in combination with tube test and WST discovered unexpected consistency of mouse social competitivity and rankings in grouped male or female mice housed in either a two- or three-member cage.
source: Interestingly, application of FPCT in combination with tube test and WST discovered unexpected consistency of mouse social competitivity and rankings in a grouped male or female mice that were housed in either a two- or three-member cage
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claim: The status sense of animals is part of a comprehensive identity of self-recognition of individuals in an established social colony.
source: most likely indicating that the status sense of animals is part of a comprehensive identity of self-recognition of individuals in an established social colony.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Social competitions occur naturally to determine the ownership or priority of living territory, food, water, mates, other resources, and non-resource requirements.
source: Social competitions occur naturally to determine the ownership or priority of living territory, food, water, mates, other resources, and non-resource requirements (Shimamoto, 2018; Korzan and Summers, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Social hierarchies from the dominant to the subordinate are established within a living group through competitions.
source: Through these competitions, social hierarchies from the dominant to the subordinate are established within a living group
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Individuals at higher social status are granted corresponding priorities of resources and non-resource requirements like living space, food availability, reproduction, and safeguard.
source: where individuals at higher social status are granted corresponding priorities of resources and non-resource requirements like living space, food availability, reproduction, and safeguard (Shimamoto, 2018; Korzan and Summers, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The establishment of dominance hierarchies reduces the intensity and frequency of mutual aggression within groups and strains.
source: The establishment of dominance hierarchies reduces the intensity and frequency of mutual aggression within groups and strains, so as to maintain their inner stability and fulfill outer assignments (Guo et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Impaired awareness of social competition has been documented in individuals with autism spectrum disorder.
source: Impaired awareness of social competition has been documented in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (Gates et al., 2017; Su et al., 2022)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reduced social interaction has been characterized in animal models of autism spectrum disorder.
source: and reduced social interaction has been characterized in corresponding animal models (Sato et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Maladaptive responses to social status loss have been associated with patient depressive disorders.
source: Similarly, maladaptive responses to social status loss have been associated with patient depressive disorders (Price et al., 1994; Komori et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Maladaptive responses to social status loss have been associated with animal models of depression.
source: and animal models of depression (Fan et al., 2023; Battivelli et al., 2024).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Rodents—particularly mice and rats—have been emerging to serve as valuable and cost-effective models for studying the biological basis of social cognition, social interaction, and social organization.
source: In contrast, rodents—particularly mice and rats—have been emerging to serve as valuable and cost-effective models for studying the biological basis of social cognition, social interaction, and social organization (Fan et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Living space, water, and food competitions are most frequently used to investigate social competitive behaviors and hierarchical ranking of rats or mice.
source: Therefore, living space, water, and food competitions are most frequently used to investigate social competitive behaviors and hierarchical ranking of rats or mice (Korzan and Summers, 2021; Goodman et al., 2021; Lucion and Vogel, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The tube test is a simple and reliable method for assessing social hierarchy by simulating the competition for living space among animals.
source: The tube test is a simple and reliable method for assessing social hierarchy by simulating the competition for living space among animals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: In the tube test, the dominant mice largely consistently squeeze out the weaker ones from the narrow tube, indicative of an overwhelming space demand of mice at higher rank.
source: In the tube test, the dominant mice largely consistently squeeze out the weaker ones from the narrow tube, indicative of an overwhelming space demand of mice at higher rank (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Warm spot test (WST) is a space competition paradigm where a pair of mice compete for a pitifully small warm corner in a freezing cage.
source: Warm spot test (WST) is another space competition paradigm where a pair of mice compete for a pitifully small warm corner in a freezing cage (Zhou et al., 2017; Zhu and Hu, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some food competition tests have been applied to animals such as rats, chickens, pigs, and mice.
source: Some food competition tests have also been applied to animals such as rats (Cordero and Sandi, 2007; Jupp et al., 2016; Timmer and Sandi, 2010), chickens (Lee et al., 1982), pigs (Hessing and Tielen, 1994), and mice (Yoon et al., 2022; Shin et al., 2022; Merlot et al., 2004; Padilla-Coreano et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Food competition procedures for rats, chickens, and pigs are difficult to be applied to mice due to their much smaller size.
source: but the food competition procedures for those animals are difficult to be applied to mice due to their much smaller size.
evidence: This is an inference based on the physical differences between species.

claim: Rats are more socially tolerant and less hierarchical than mice.
source: but rats are more socially tolerant and less hierarchical than mice (Kim et al., 2015; Bartos and Brain, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Food competition tests for mice have been designated and applied less commonly in animal studies despite its long history.
source: Relative to space competition, food competition tests for mice have been designated and applied less commonly in animal studies despite its long history (Fredericson, 1950; Fredericson, 1952; Schuhr, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and represents an observation about the field.

claim: There are methodological issues in some food competition approaches, such as long video recording duration and difficulty in analyzing animals' behaviors during competitive physical interaction in videos.
source: First, there are methodological issues in some of these approaches, such as long video recording duration and difficulty in analyzing animals' behaviors during competitive physical interaction in videos, hindering their application by laboratories that cannot afford sophisticated equipment (Shin et al., 2022; Merlot et al., 2004; Li et al., 2007; Timmer and Sandi, 2010; Löfgren et al., 2013; Costa et al., 2021) and analysis (Li et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Aggressive behaviors often occur during competition in food competition approaches as the mice compete in a shared arena.
source: Second, aggressive behaviors often occur during competition in these approaches as the mice compete in a shared arena.
evidence: This is an observation about existing methods supported by citations.

claim: Prolonged food deprivation is usually required to increase the effortful food competition.
source: Third, the prolonged food deprivation is usually required to increase the effortful food competition.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of existing food competition paradigms.

claim: Aggressiveness/being aggressed and intense food deprivation cause stress responses and changes of physiological state of animals.
source: For the second and third issues, on one hand, the aggressiveness/being aggressed and intense food deprivation cause stress responses and changes of physiological state of animals (Battivelli et al., 2024; Merlot et al., 2004; Fredericson, 1950; Fredericson, 1952).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Competition in the same arena conflates multiple determinants contributing to the outcomes of competition involving physical aspects and psychological aspects.
source: On the other hand, competition in the same arena conflates multiple determinants contributing to the outcomes of competition involving physical aspects—such as muscular strength, vigorousness of fighting, bite wounding—and psychological aspects—such as boldness, focused motivation, active self-awareness of status.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of existing competition paradigms.

claim: Food competition tasks had not been conceived to separate the physical aspects from psychological aspects interpreting the mice's winning/losing.
source: So far, the food competition tasks had not been conceived to separate the physical aspects from psychological aspects interpreting the mice's winning/losing.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of existing methods.

claim: FPCT did not detect significant difference in the winning/losing results between unfamiliar non-cagemate male mice.
source: Statistical data found that daily average scores acquired by the two groups of mice were not significantly different (Figure 1J), illustrating that no nonsocial priority-associated competition factor was obviously involved in the FPCT with the sex-, age-, and weight-controlled unfamiliar mice.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: It took 4–5 days for the mice to learn to walk straightforwardly to the obstacle once they entered the chamber and move the block easily to expose the food pellet.
source: Usually, it took 4–5 days for the mice to learn to walk straightforwardly to the obstacle once they entered the chamber and move the block easily to expose the food pellet (Figure 1E, Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the training phase of the experiment.

claim: The orientation of the entries did not generate bias of performance of mice in the apparatus.
source: The orientation of the entries did not generate bias of performance of mice in the apparatus (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Winners and losers displayed the same level of training to get the food, indicating equivalent motivational craving for the food.
source: Retrograde analysis of the time spent to get the food after entering the arena gate in the last day of training showed that the winners and losers displayed the same level of training to get the food, indicating equivalent motivational craving for the food (Figure 2A, day –1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of training data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: When there was competition in the test, the winners tended to win the pellet over all the four trials.
source: However, when there was competition in the test, the winners tended to win the pellet over all the four trials (Figure 2A, days 1–4).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The presence of an opponent during the test did not significantly change the latency to get the food, comparing with the last day of training when there was no opponent.
source: Notably, the presence of an opponent during the test did not significantly change the latency to get the food, comparing with the last day of training when there was no opponent (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In all the 16 pairs of mice, only 1 pair exhibited alternating winning/losing outcomes with an inter-trial consistency at 50%.
source: In all the 16 pairs of mice, only 1 pair exhibited alternating winning/losing outcomes with an inter-trial consistency at 50% (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All the other 15 pairs kept 100% consistency of winning/losing readouts.
source: while all the other 15 pairs kept 100% consistency of winning/losing readouts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A rate of consistency reached 96.88% in the FPCT for two-cagemate male mice.
source: and a rate of consistency reached 96.88% (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a calculated result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The winners determined by the final trial of test 1 tried harder to get the food pellet by spending more time to push the block within the single 2 min test.
source: In test 2 (indirect win-lose test via analyzing mouse's attempt to gain the food), we observed that the winners determined by the final trial of test 1 tried harder to get the food pellet by spending more time to push the block within the single 2 min test, a limited time to avoid distinction of attempt (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Consecutive four trials (one trial daily) might be least required for the FPCT to achieve readout consistency and reliability.
source: Thus, these data demonstrate that FPCTs are effective to rank the established social status of mice, and that consecutive four trials (one trial daily) might be least required for the FPCT to achieve readout consistency and reliability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results.

claim: There was no difference between the winners and losers in weight measured after finishing the food competition tests.
source: and no difference between the winners and losers in weight measured again after finishing the food competition tests (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Retrospective comparison of the duration mice took to obtain the food pellets in the last day of training reported no difference in the latency to get the food pellet between the winners and losers.
source: Third, biased training level should produce distinct likelihood of winning and losing, but retrospective comparison of the duration they took to obtain the food pellets in the last day of training—when there was no competition—reported no difference in the latency to get the food pellet between the winners and losers (Figure 2A), indicating that the mice were equally trained and motivated.
evidence: This is based on analysis of training data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The winning/losing outcomes in the FPCT paradigm mainly rely on mice's state of psychological factors.
source: Thus, we postulated that the winning/losing outcomes in this paradigm mainly rely on mice's state of psychological factors, e.g., intensity of motivation, self-awareness of social status, memory of winning/losing experience in the homecage, fear of revenge when returning the living cage.
evidence: This is a postulation based on the elimination of other factors.

claim: Self-awareness of social status plays a determinant role in the outcomes of FPCT.
source: Most likely, self-awareness of social status plays a determinant role in the outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design and results.

claim: Consistency of outcomes between the FPCT and tube test was 100% for two-cagemate male mice.
source: We found that consistency of outcomes between the FPCT and tube test was 100%, as the winners and losers in the last trial of the FPCT continued consecutively to be the winners and losers, respectively, during the four consecutive trials of tube tests (Figure 2I and J).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 2I and J.

claim: The rank order examined by the FPCT is fully verified by the tube test.
source: Therefore, the rank order examined by the FPCT is fully verified by the tube test.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the 100% consistency between FPCT and tube test results.

claim: 3 in 10 pairs of cagemate female mice exhibited alternating winning/losing outcomes in FPCT.
source: Notably, the FPCT test 1 showed that 3 in 10 pairs of cagemate female mice exhibited alternating winning/losing outcomes, while the majority of cagemates (7 in 10 pairs) showed fully congruent grades (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 3A-E.

claim: The majority of female cagemate pairs (7 in 10 pairs) showed fully congruent grades in FPCT.
source: while the majority of cagemates (7 in 10 pairs) showed fully congruent grades (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 3A-E.

claim: 10 female pairs displayed stable rankings throughout all trials in FPCT.
source: On average, 10 female pairs displayed stable rankings throughout all trials (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The overall rate of inter-trial consistency was 90% for female mice in FPCT.
source: The overall rate of inter-trial consistency was 90% (Figure 3G), which was not significantly different from that of male mice (p>0.05 comparing data in Figure 2E and G using Mann-Whitney U test).
evidence: This is a calculated result from the experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Winner mice in test 1 made more efforts trying to get the food pellet in test 2.
source: In test 2, we observed that winner mice in test 1 made more efforts trying to get the food pellet (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The body weights examined after the tests were similar between the winners and losers in female mice.
source: The body weights examined after the tests (Figure 3I) were similar between the winners and losers, so the weight parameters were not likely to contribute to the competency.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Retrospective analysis of training data displayed similar training level of food-getting and craving state for food in female mice.
source: Interestingly, retrospective analysis of training data displayed similar training level of food-getting and craving state for food (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of training data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The social relationship of female mice is stratified.
source: These FPCT results suggest that the social relationship of female mice is also stratified.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the FPCT results for female mice.

claim: No difference was observed in the rate of inter-trial consistency comparing FPCT with tube test, FPCT with WST, and tube test with WST for female mice.
source: Overall, no difference was observed in the rate of inter-trial consistency comparing FPCT with tube test, FPCT with WST, and tube test with WST (Figure 3N).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 3N.

claim: Mouse social competency and status of established female mice colony are overall stable so that a well-competitive subject exhibits dominance not just in a specific, but in a variety of contexts.
source: These data illustrate that mouse social competency and status of established female mice colony are overall stable so that a well-competitive subject exhibits dominance not just in a specific, but in a variety of contexts, despite that the different contexts contain distinct competitive factors like food and space, or competitive aspects like physical strength and psychological factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the consistency of rankings across different tests.

claim: Six in nine groups of three-cagemate male mice displayed some extent of flipped ranking across FPCT, tube test, and WST.
source: The ranking result showed that six in nine groups of mice displayed some extent of flipped ranking (Figure 4B–G), and only three in nine groups displayed continuously unaltered ranking (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figures 4B-H.

claim: Only three in nine groups of three-cagemate male mice displayed continuously unaltered ranking across FPCT, tube test, and WST.
source: and only three in nine groups displayed continuously unaltered ranking (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: An obvious stable linear intragroup hierarchy was observed across all the trials and tasks for three-cagemate male mice.
source: On average, in the total of 27 trials consisting of 12 trials of FPCT, 12 trials of tube test, and 3 trials of WST, an obvious stable linear intragroup hierarchy was observed across all the trials and tasks (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figures 4I and J.

claim: The ranks assessed by FPCT, tube test, and WST did not differ from each other for three-cagemate male mice.
source: Comparison of inter-task consistency revealed that the ranks assessed by FPCT, tube test, and WST did not differ from each other (FPCT vs tube test, 85.19+17.95%; FPCT vs WST, 81.59+17.95%; tube test vs WST, 81.48+17.95%; p>0.05, one-way ANOVA test; Figure 4K).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The dominant and subordinate roles in an established group of mice are rigorously linearly stratified so that the status can be manifested in various contexts.
source: These results, together with the results of female mice tested by FPCT, tube test, and WST, illustrate that the dominant and subordinate roles in an established group of mice are rigorously linearly stratified so that the status can be manifested in various contexts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the consistency of rankings across different tests and group sizes.

claim: Mice have been designated to participate in food competition tests for a long time, since at least the 1950s.
source: Mice have been designated to participate in food competition tests for a long time, since at least the 1950s (Fredericson, 1950; Fredericson, 1952).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In applied food competition tests, social ranks were scored by calculating the total amount of food consumed by each mouse competing in the same chamber or cage and/or analyzing their physical aggressiveness.
source: In these applied food competition tests, social ranks were scored by calculating the total amount of food consumed by each mouse competing in the same chamber or cage and/or analyzing their physical aggressiveness (Yoon et al., 2022; Shin et al., 2022; Schuhr, 1987; Williamson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Food shortage serves as a strong driver to induce aggressiveness and competitive behaviors.
source: Food shortage serves as a strong driver to induce aggressiveness and competitive behaviors (Tucci et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In rodents, being physically aggressed and undergoing intense food deprivation can influence social competitive behaviors via disturbing the internal state.
source: However, in rodents, being physically aggressed and undergoing intense food deprivation can influence social competitive behaviors via disturbing the internal state (Merlot et al., 2004; Li et al., 2007; Márquez et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Being physically aggressed and undergoing intense food deprivation can trigger robust stress responses in rodents.
source: and triggering robust stress responses (Tucci et al., 2006; Márquez et al., 2013; Kennedy and Shapiro, 2009; Reppucci et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mice underwent only a 24 hr food deprivation period at the beginning of training in FPCT.
source: The potential influence of food restriction on competitive behavior was minimized in our task where the mice underwent only a 24 hr food deprivation period at the beginning of training, followed by restricted food supply to meet basic energy requirements.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The aggressive situations, at least direct physical fighting, were prevented during FPCT ranking test due to the separation of the mice on either side of the arena.
source: The aggressive situations, at least direct physical fighting, were prevented during this ranking test due to the separation of the mice on either side of the arena.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design feature.

claim: Stable social hierarchy relies on adequate habituation.
source: Importantly to note, stable social hierarchy relies on adequate habituation, and reliable ranking test is based on well training.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for the experimental design.

claim: Reliable ranking test is based on well training.
source: Importantly to note, stable social hierarchy relies on adequate habituation, and reliable ranking test is based on well training.
evidence: This is stated as a principle for the experimental design.

claim: Both static vs dynamic and linear vs despotic hierarchy organizations of grouped mice have been documented.
source: Concerning the interpretation of the ranking results, both static vs dynamic and linear vs despotic hierarchy organizations of grouped mice have been documented (Costa et al., 2021; Varholick et al., 2019; Williamson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both correlation and noncorrelation between weight and hierarchy have been reported.
source: It is not sure if body size/weight affects social hierarchy as both correlation (Costa et al., 2021) and noncorrelation (Battivelli et al., 2024; Williamson et al., 2016) between weight and hierarchy have been reported.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature showing conflicting results.

claim: The majority of female pairs displayed overall stable hierarchy ranks.
source: First, we found that the majority of female pairs displayed overall stable hierarchy ranks, consistent with previous findings (Smith-Osborne et al., 2023; LeClair et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 3 in 10 female cagemate pairs exhibited fluctuant rankings during the 4-day FPCT test.
source: We also detected 3 in 10 female cagemate pairs exhibiting fluctuant rankings during the 4-day FPCT test, but it was not significant from 1 in 16 male pairs.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: Female social hierarchies are not as steep and despotic as male hierarchies.
source: It has been revealed by agonistic behaviors in previous work that female social hierarchies are not as steep and despotic as male hierarchies (Williamson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Both FPCT and tube test detected averagely linear intragroup hierarchies in three-cagemate mice.
source: Second, by means of round-robin tests of multiple cagemates, both FPCT and tube test detected averagely linear intragroup hierarchies, consistent with each other.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The ranking readouts of male pairs and triads examined by FPCT, tube test, and WST were highly consistent with each other.
source: Third, considering that diverse competitive factors lie in different tasks, the ranking readouts of male pairs and triads examined by FPCT, tube test, and WST were highly consistent with each other, revealing social rank-order stability of mice across the three types of examining tasks.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The fluctuation of the rankings occurs occasionally, suggesting that the social status of mice could be dynamic and transitive on some occasions.
source: Notably, the fluctuation of the rankings occurs occasionally, suggesting that the social status of mice could be dynamic and transitive on some occasions (Varholick et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings supported by a citation.

claim: Hierarchical sense of animals might be part of a comprehensive identity of self-recognition of individuals within an established social colony.
source: In conclusion, our data suggest that hierarchical sense of animals might be part of a comprehensive identity of self-recognition of individuals within an established social colony.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The mice used in this study were 6- to 8-week-old C57BL/6JNifdc purchased from SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Company.
source: The mice used in this study were 6- to 8-week-old C57BL/6JNifdc purchased from SPF (Beijing) Biotechnology Company (Beijing, China)
evidence: This is a description of the experimental materials.

claim: The mice were raised in the environment with the relative humidity 50–75%, temperature 22–24°C, and 12–12 hr light-dark cycle.
source: and were raised in the environment with the relative humidity 50–75%, temperature 22–24°C, and 12–12 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: Contender pair of C57BL/6JNifdc mice with similar age and weight (the weight difference was less than 10%) were housed in the same cage for at least 3 days.
source: Contender pair of C57BL/6JNifdc mice with similar age and weight (the weight difference was less than 10%) were housed in the same cage for at least 3 days under a 12–12 hr light-dark cycle.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: The mice were deprived of food for 24 hr to enhance the appeal of the food pellet to the mice while water consumption remained normal.
source: First, the mice were deprived of food for 24 hr to enhance the appeal of the food pellet to the mice while water consumption remained normal.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: After 24 hr of food deprivation, each cage of mice was given 5 g/mouse of food every morning to meet their daily food requirements until the end of the test.
source: Then, after 24 hr of food deprivation, each cage of mice was given 5 g/mouse of food every morning to meet their daily food requirements until the end of the test.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.
